h1: AI agents vs chatbots vs RPA: what each one actually does in a business
answer_first: The short answer to AI agents vs chatbots vs RPA: all three automate work, but they do different jobs. RPA follows a fixed script across screens and systems. A chatbot answers questions in a conversation. An AI agent takes a request, decides the steps within your rules, acts inside your systems and records what it did.
body_html:
The short answer to AI agents vs chatbots vs RPA: all three automate work, but they do different jobs. RPA follows a fixed script across screens and systems. A chatbot answers questions in a conversation. An AI agent takes a request, decides the steps within your rules, acts inside your systems and records what it did. Most real setups use more than one, so the useful question is which job each one should own.

This guide compares the three where it matters when something goes wrong: memory, decisions, actions in your systems and failure modes.

What changed recently?

The word "agent" is now on almost every automation product, and analysts have started to push back. Gartner calls the practice "agent washing": rebranding AI assistants, RPA and chatbots as agentic when they lack real agentic features. It estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors selling agentic AI are real, and it predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of cost, unclear value or weak risk controls (Gartner).

At the same time, the large platforms are drawing the line in the same place: the control layer. On October 13, 2026, Workday said every agent on its platform, whether built by Workday, a customer or a partner, "works under the same Workday permissions, approvals, and audit trails" (Workday).

In September, Rocket Software put a policy and identity check between its mainframe agents' reasoning and their actions, with every action logged for audits (ITdaily). For buyers, the lesson is that the rules, permissions and record around an agent separate it from a chatbot with integrations more than the model does.

AI agents vs chatbots vs RPA: what is the difference?

The clearest way to compare AI agents vs chatbots vs RPA is to ask each one the same seven questions.

RPA botChatbotAI agent
Starts fromA trigger or schedule with structured input (a file, a form, a queue item)A message from a personA request or event on any channel, structured or not
Decides byFixed steps and if/then rules written in advanceA script or decision tree, or a language model that writes a replyA language model that plans steps, checked against business rules and limits
RemembersNothing between runs, apart from logsThe current conversation, sometimes a short historyThe customer or employee, past conversations and the state of open tasks
Can changeAnything its login can reach, exactly as scriptedUsually nothing, or one or two narrow actionsRecords, bookings, messages and tasks in connected systems, within permissions
When input changesStops or does the wrong thingFalls back to "I didn't understand" or guessesAdapts, asks a question or hands off
Typical failureBreaks after a screen or format changeGives a confident wrong answerTakes a wrong or unapproved action
Best atHigh-volume, stable, rule-based back-office stepsAnswering common questions fastVariable requests that need judgment and work across systems

Each column to the right handles messier input, and each one also fails in a new way. That is why controls matter more the closer you get to agents.

How does RPA work, and where does it break?

Robotic process automation (RPA) is software that repeats the clicks and keystrokes a person makes in business applications. A developer records or builds the steps: open the invoice queue, copy the amount, paste it into the accounting system, mark the item done. The bot then runs those steps the same way every time.

That determinism is RPA's strength. For stable, high-volume work with clean input, an RPA bot is predictable and easy to audit, because it only ever does what the script says.

The weakness is the same determinism. RPA bots locate fields by their position or attributes on the screen, so a redesigned page, a renamed column or a new pop-up can stop them. They also cannot read intent: an email asking to change last week's delivery address means nothing to a bot built for a structured form. Exceptions go to a queue for a person to clear.

What does a chatbot actually do?

A chatbot is software that holds a conversation. Older chatbots follow a decision tree with buttons and keywords. Newer ones use a large language model to understand free text and write answers from a knowledge base.

Either way, a chatbot's main output is a reply. Some can look up an order status, but most stop at information or a link.

The main failure is a fluent, wrong answer, and the business owns it. In Moffatt v. Air Canada (February 2024), the airline's website chatbot told a customer he could apply for a bereavement fare after travel, which contradicted the airline's own policy page.

Air Canada argued it was not liable for what the chatbot said. The tribunal called that "a remarkable submission," found the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation and ordered it to pay $812.02 in damages, interest and fees (Civil Resolution Tribunal). The payout was small, but the principle is not: whatever an automated assistant tells a customer on your website counts as your answer.

What makes an AI agent different?

An AI agent is software that takes a goal, decides the steps, uses tools to carry them out and checks the result. In a business, a working agent is built from five parts:

  1. A model that understands the request and plans the next step.
  2. Tools, meaning connections to the CRM, calendar, billing or phone system. Open standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) give agents a common way to discover and call these tools and read data from them (MCP specification).
  3. Memory of who is asking, what happened before and which tasks are still open.
  4. Rules that say what the agent may do alone, what needs a person and what it never does.
  5. A record of every action, the rule that applied and who approved it.

Take away the rules and the record and you have a chatbot that can press buttons. Take away the model and you have RPA.

What does each one do with the same request?

Here is one email, sent to a fictional dental clinic, handled three ways. The clinic and the customer are made up for illustration.

"Hi, I need to move my Thursday cleaning to next week, and the last invoice has my old address. Also, can you take off the late fee? I paid two days late because of the address mix-up."

SystemWhat happens
RPA botNothing, unless the email matches a template it was built for. The message lands in the exception queue for staff.
ChatbotReplies with a link to the booking page, explains how to update an address and says fee questions go to billing.
AI agentFinds the patient record, offers two open slots next week and books the one the patient picks. Updates the billing address. The late fee is above what the agent may waive alone, so it asks the office manager, then confirms the result to the patient. Every step is logged.

Nothing in the agent's column is clever. It is what a good front-desk employee would do, held to the same limits the clinic would give that employee.

How does each one fail, and how do you contain it?

Every automation fails sometimes. What you can control is how big a failure gets before someone notices it.

SystemHow it failsHow to contain it
RPA botStops or enters wrong data after a system change; exceptions pile up unseenMonitoring and alerts on failed runs, an owner for the exception queue, regression tests after each system update
ChatbotAnswers wrongly or makes up a policyAnswers only from approved documents, a clear handoff to a person, regular review of transcripts
AI agentTakes an action it should not, or too many actionsLeast-privilege access, approval for high-impact actions, spending and refund limits, an audit log with the rule behind each action

The agent row matches what the OWASP security project calls "excessive agency": damaging actions caused by giving an AI system too much functionality, too many permissions or too much autonomy. Its main recommendations are to grant the minimum permissions needed and to "require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken" (OWASP).

Which one should your business use?

Start from the shape of the work. The product label tells you very little.

  • Use RPA when the steps never change, the input is structured and the target system has no API. Nightly data transfers and form filling in legacy software are good fits.
  • Use a chatbot when the job is answering common questions and the answer does not require changing anything.
  • Use an AI agent when requests arrive in free text or by voice, vary from case to case and need work in more than one system, such as booking, updating records, billing and follow-up.

They also combine. An agent can treat an existing RPA bot as one of its tools, for example to enter data in an old system with no API, while the agent handles the conversation, the decisions and the approvals. That way the bots you already paid for keep running, and the agent covers the parts they could never handle.

How can you tell if a vendor is selling a real AI agent?

Given how much agent washing is going on, ask these six questions in any demo:

  1. Show me a request the system has never seen. What does it do?
  2. Which systems can it change, and where do I set its permissions?
  3. How do I set what it does alone, what needs approval and what it never does?
  4. What does it remember about a customer across channels and weeks?
  5. When it is unsure, how does it hand off, and does the person see the full history?
  6. Show me the log for one action: the request, the rule that applied and who approved it.

A renamed chatbot struggles with questions 2, 3 and 6. Renamed RPA struggles with question 1.

Where does an AI operating system fit?

Most businesses need many small jobs done across sales, service and operations, all under the same rules. An AI operating system for business is one layer of agents with one memory of each customer and employee, one set of rules and one record.

That is how Aurora is built. Requests come in by phone, SMS, web chat, email, WhatsApp or Slack, and Aurora acts inside your CRM, calendar and other systems. You choose what Aurora does on its own, what needs a person's approval and what it never does, and every action is written to the audit log.

Frequently asked questions

Is a chatbot with integrations an AI agent?

A chatbot with integrations is not an AI agent unless it can plan several steps toward a goal, act in those systems on its own and work within rules you set. If it can only fetch information or run one fixed action per question, it is still a chatbot.

Will AI agents replace RPA?

AI agents will take over many tasks that RPA handled badly, such as reading emails and handling exceptions. RPA will stay useful for stable, high-volume steps in systems without an API, often called by an agent as one of its tools.

Are AI agents riskier than chatbots?

AI agents carry a different risk than chatbots because they can change records, not only say things. That risk is managed with least-privilege access, approval for high-impact actions and a full audit log, which together make an agent's mistakes small and visible.

Next steps

The difference between AI agents vs chatbots vs RPA comes down to who decides and who checks. With RPA, the script decided months ago. Most chatbots never act at all. An AI agent decides in the moment, which is only safe when your rules limit it and the log shows what it did.
